title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 Arminius parallel: Exam. Perkins — soft persuasion not coercion; same Pelagian calumny; Corvinus leaves the will at the fork
pass_a_gloss: And hence it is that from God’s foresight, by which from eternity he knows whether a man will let in knocking grace or not, they establish that election and reprobation proceed. Let us hear Arminius himself, Exam. Praedest. Perkin. pag. 220. The Author of grace has established by his grace not to compel men unto assenting, but to move them by gentle and sweet persuasion. This is the same which Pelagius granted: He persuades everything that is good. That also is to be observed: that Arminius hints that If Divine grace act otherwise than by this gentle persuasion, by which it leaves the event unto free will, it at once compels the will: which was the very calumny of Pelagius and the Semipelagians. But let us join Corvinus also unto Arminius; who acknowledges no other grace than that which leaves the will as it were set at a fork, so that if the will by its own act is carried unto that unto which grace allures, then the man is converted; but if otherwise, he is left inexcusable.
pass_b_english: Hence they let election and reprobation proceed from God’s foresight of whether a man will admit knocking grace or not. Hear Arminius himself (Exam. Praedest. Perkins, p. 220): The Author of grace has set that by his grace he will not compel men to assent, but move them by gentle, sweet persuasion. That is what Pelagius granted: He persuades all that is good. Note also Arminius’s hint: if divine grace acts otherwise than by this soft persuasion that leaves the event to free will, it at once compels the will—the very calumny of Pelagius and the Semipelagians. Join Corvinus to Arminius: he acknowledges no grace but what leaves the will at a fork—so that if the will by its own act goes where grace allures, the man is converted; if not, he is left without excuse.
source_text: Atque hinc est quod ex praescientia Dei, qua ab aeterno cognoscit velitne homo gratiam pulsantem intromittere an secus, procedere statuant electionem et reprobationem. Audiamus ipsum Arminium, Exam. Praedest. Perkin. pag. 220. Gratiae Autor statuit per gratiam suam non cogere homines ad assentiendum, sed leni et suavi suasione movere. Hoc idem est quod concessit Pelagius: Suadet omne quod bonum est. Illud etiam observandum: Innuere Arminium, Si Divina gratia aliter agat quam per hanc lenem suasionem, qua eventum relinquit libero arbitrio, illam protinus cogere voluntatem: quae fuit ipsissima Pelagii et Semipelagianorum calumnia. Sed Arminio jungamus etiam Corvinum; qui aliam gratiam non agnoscit, praeter eam quae voluntatem in bivio quasi positam relinquit, ita ut si voluntas suo actu in id feratur ad quod allicit gratia, tum homo convertatur; sin secus, inexcusabilis relinquatur.
